answer: For a fixed mortgage payment to fall from 35% to 28% of pay, pay must rise 25%. Using average hourly pay since 1964, that took a median of 82 months (about 7 years) across 691 start months; the fastest was 34 months (starting December 1977, high inflation) and the slowest 120. For start months since 1990 the median was 86 months, it never took 48 months or less, and the fastest was 52. Five years in, the payment was still a median 30.0% of pay. History, not a forecast.
guess: Buyers stretching to 35% often assume a few years of raises (three or four) will bring the payment back to a comfortable 28%.
changesDecision: Average pay has not grown fast enough since 1990 to make a 35% payment a 28% payment in four years; the typical wait is about seven years and the payment is still near 30% after five. A buyer can compare that path with their own raise expectations before counting on raises to fix the stretch.

assumptions: The mortgage payment is fixed (principal and interest); taxes and insurance, which usually rise, are not included.
The buyer's pay grows like the national average hourly earnings of production and nonsupervisory workers; promotions, job changes and career stage are not modeled.
Gross pay; no change in hours or household earners.
limits: History, not a forecast. An average across workers is not an individual raise path: early-career workers and job changers often see faster growth, others slower or none. Rising property taxes and insurance make the true housing share fall more slowly than shown. Hourly earnings series covers production and nonsupervisory employees only.
